title: The plan behind an average
hook: Two toy project outcomes share the same expected score. What can the mean hide?

knows: basic arithmetic and the meaning of a percentage
doesNotKnow: Inspect lower outcome branches before using an expected score as a description of project risk.

misconception: An equal expected project score implies equal downside exposure.
objective: Inspect lower outcome branches before using an expected score as a description of project risk.

claims.text: Waltzing with Bears argues for acknowledging uncertainty instead of treating a single project estimate as a guarantee.
claims.source: Tom DeMarco and Timothy Lister, Waltzing with Bears (2003); chapter (unconfirmed); edition and bibliography not independently opened. Access hold F1.

claims.text: Original stipulated payoff model: A inputs [50, 20, 0] yield 10; B inputs [50, 50, -30] yield 10. Prediction correct option 10.00. Both A and B average {A} points. B can still lose 30, while A’s lower branch is zero; equal means do not erase downside. Scores are invented net outcomes, not durations or a deadline-risk distribution.
claims.source: Original lesson construction; EDD-010 formula ; exact independent Python arithmetic recomputation recorded in answerCheck; no book dataset or measured human response.

claims.text: A toy plan has equal chances of net +30 and −10 schedule points. Its expected score? 0.5 × 30 + 0.5 × (−10) = 10; the mean does not eliminate the −10 branch.
claims.source: Original transfer toy, payoff, inputs [50, 30, -10], output 10; independent Python recomputation.
